user_input: I have a flaky test I'd like re-run a couple of times on failure — what's the quickest command-line way?
reference: Pass a retry count on the run command, e.g. npx playwright test --retries=3 re-runs failing tests up to three times. Nothing is retried unless you opt in.
reference_contexts: Playwright supports test retries . When enabled, failing tests will be retried multiple times until they pass, or until the maximum number of retries is reached. By default failing tests are not retried.
llm_response:
The quickest command-line way to re-run failing tests is to use the `--retries` flag with the `npx playwright test` command.

For example, to give failing tests 3 retry attempts, use:
`npx playwright test --retries=3`
llm_references: Retries | Playwright

Command line | Playwright

Playwright provides a powerful command line interface for running tests, generating code, debugging, and more. The most up to date list of commands and arguments available on the CLI can always be retrieved via
`npx playwright --help`
.

Playwright supports
test retries
. When enabled, failing tests will be retried multiple times until they pass, or until the maximum number of retries is reached. By default failing tests are not retried.

```
`# Give failing tests 3 retry attemptsnpx playwrighttest--retries=3`
```

You can configure retries in the configuration file:

playwright.config.ts
```
`import{defineConfig}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({// Give failing tests 3 retry attemptsretries:3,});`
```

Playwright Test will categorize tests as follows:

"passed" - tests that passed on the first run;
"flaky" - tests that failed on the first run, but passed when retried;
"failed" - tests that failed on the first run and failed all retries.

```
`Running3tests using1worker✓ example.spec.ts:4:2 › first passes(438ms)x example.spec.ts:5:2 › second flaky(691ms)✓ example.spec.ts:5:2 › second flaky(522ms)✓ example.spec.ts:6:2 › third passes(932ms)1flakyexample.spec.ts:5:2 › second flaky2passed(4s)`
```

You can detect retries at runtime with
testInfo.retry (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testinfo#test-info-retry)
, which is accessible to any test, hook or fixture. Here is an example that clears some server-side state before a retry.

```
`import{test,expect}from'@playwright/test';test('my test',async({page},testInfo)=>{if(testInfo.retry)awaitcleanSomeCachesOnTheServer();// ...});`
```

You can specify retries for a specific group of tests or a single file with
test.describe.configure() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-test#test-describe-configure)
.

```
`import{test,expect}from'@playwright/test';test.describe(()=>{// All tests in this describe group will get 2 retry attempts.test.describe.configure({retries:2});test('test 1',async({page})=>{// ...});test('test 2',async({page})=>{// ...});});`
```

user_input: Do I get videos of my test runs automatically, or do I have to switch them on?
reference: They stay off unless you opt in; a single config setting — video — turns recording on and selects the mode.
reference_contexts: Playwright Test can record videos for your tests, controlled by the video option in your Playwright config. By default videos are off.
llm_references: Videos | Playwright

Playwright Test can record videos for your tests, controlled by the
`video`
option in your Playwright config. By default videos are off.

`'off'`
- Do not record video.
`'on'`
- Record video for each test.
`'retain-on-failure'`
- Record video for each test, but remove all videos from successful test runs.
`'on-first-retry'`
- Record video only when retrying a test for the first time.

Video files will appear in the test output directory, typically
`test-results`
. See
testOptions.video (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testoptions#test-options-video)
for advanced video configuration.

Videos are saved upon
browser context (https://playwright.dev/docs/browser-contexts)
closure at the end of a test. If you create a browser context manually, make sure to await
browserContext.close() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsercontext#browser-context-close)
.

Test
Library
playwright.config.ts
```
`import{defineConfig}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({use:{video:'on-first-retry',},});`
```
```
`constcontext=awaitbrowser.newContext({recordVideo:{dir:'videos/'}});// Make sure to await close, so that videos are saved.awaitcontext.close();`
```

You can also specify video size and annotation. The video size defaults to the viewport size scaled down to fit 800x800. The video of the viewport is placed in the top-left corner of the output video, scaled down to fit if necessary. You may need to set the viewport size to match your desired video size.

When
`show: { actions }`

`duration`
property controls how long each annotation is displayed (defaults to
`500`

When

```
`import{defineConfig}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({use:{video:{mode:'on-first-retry',size:{width:640,height:480},show:{actions:{duration:500,position:'top-right',fontSize:14,},test:{level:'step',position:'top-left',fontSize:12,}},},},});`
```

For multi-page scenarios, you can access the video file associated with the page via the

user_input: If my selector happens to match several elements and I try to click, what does Playwright do?
reference: It refuses to guess — locators are strict, so any action that needs one element throws when the locator resolves to more than one.
reference_contexts: Locators are strict. This means that all operations on locators that imply some target DOM element will throw an exception if more than one element matches. For example, the following call throws if there are several buttons in the DOM:
llm_response:
If your selector matches several elements, Playwright throws an exception when you perform an operation that implies a single target DOM element, such as `.click()` [1, 2].

To resolve this, you can use the following methods to explicitly select a single element, though these are not recommended as they may lead to unintended clicks if the page changes:
*   `locator.first()`
*   `locator.last()`
*   `locator.nth()`

The documentation recommends instead creating a locator that uniquely identifies the target element [3].
llm_references: Locators are strict. This means that all operations on locators that imply some target DOM element will throw an exception if more than one element matches. For example, the following call throws if there are several buttons in the DOM:

```
`awaitpage.getByRole('button').click();`
```

On the other hand, Playwright understands when you perform a multiple-element operation, so the following call works perfectly fine when the locator resolves to multiple elements.

```
`awaitpage.getByRole('button').count();`
```

You can explicitly opt-out from strictness check by telling Playwright which element to use when multiple elements match, through
locator.first() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-first)
,
locator.last() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-last)
, and
locator.nth() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-nth)
. These methods are
not recommended
because when your page changes, Playwright may click on an element you did not intend. Instead, follow best practices above to create a locator that uniquely identifies the target element.

user_input: If my page throws up an alert or confirm and I never handle it, will my test get stuck?
reference: No — with no dialog listener registered, Playwright dismisses dialogs automatically, so they won't block the run.
reference_contexts: If there is no listener for page.on('dialog') (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-event-dialog) , all dialogs are automatically dismissed.
llm_response:
No, your test will not get stuck if you do not handle the dialog. By default, Playwright automatically dismisses dialogs if there is no `page.on('dialog')` listener registered.

However, if you do register a `page.on('dialog')` listener, you must explicitly call `dialog.accept()` or `dialog.dismiss()`. If you register a listener but fail to perform one of these actions, the page will freeze and your test actions will stall.

user_input: What's the pattern to trigger a file download and save it where I want?
reference: Arm the 'download' wait before the click (don't await it yet), click, await the download, then saveAs() using suggestedFilename().
llm_response:
To trigger a file download and save it to a specific location, the recommended pattern is to wait for the `download` event before performing the action that initiates the download.

### Recommended Pattern
1. **Start waiting for the download** using `page.waitForEvent('download')` before triggering the action (e.g., clicking a button). Do not use `await` on this line.
2. **Perform the action** that triggers the download.
3. **Await the download promise** to obtain the `Download` object.
4. **Save the file** using the `download.saveAs()` method, providing your desired path and the `download.suggestedFilename()` to maintain the original file name.

**Example:**
```javascript
// Start waiting for download before clicking. Note no await.
const downloadPromise = page.waitForEvent('download');
await page.getByText('Download file').click();
const download = await downloadPromise;

// Wait for the download process to complete and save the downloaded file somewhere.
await download.saveAs('/path/to/save/at/' + download.suggestedFilename());
```

### Alternative Configuration
You can also specify a persistent directory for all downloads by using the `downloadsPath` option when launching the browser:
```javascript
browserType.launch({ downloadsPath: '/path/to/save/at/' });
```

### Important Considerations
* **Temporary Storage:** By default, files are downloaded into a temporary folder and are deleted when the browser context that produced them is closed.
* **`saveAs` behavior:** This method is safe to call while the download is still in progress; it will wait for the download to finish if necessary.
* **Event Handling:** While you can use `page.on('download', ...)` to handle downloads, this forks the control flow and is generally discouraged because the main script may finish before the download completes.

```

user_input: Where should I keep saved login state, and how do I keep it out of version control?
reference: Stash it in a playwright/.auth directory and add that folder to .gitignore; tests then reuse the saved state to start already signed in.
reference_contexts: We recommend to create playwright/.auth directory and add it to your .gitignore . Your authentication routine will produce authenticated browser state and save it to a file in this playwright/.auth directory. Later on, tests will reuse this state and start already authenticated.
llm_response:
You should store authenticated browser state in a directory named `playwright/.auth` on the file system.

To keep this state out of version control, you must add the `playwright/.auth` directory to your `.gitignore` file. You can do this using the following commands:

*   **Bash:** `mkdir -p playwright/.auth && echo $'\nplaywright/.auth' >> .gitignore`
*   **PowerShell:** `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path playwright\.auth; Add-Content -Path .gitignore "`r`nplaywright/.auth"`
*   **Batch:** `md playwright\.auth && echo. >> .gitignore && echo "playwright/.auth" >> .gitignore`

Checking these files into repositories is strongly discouraged because they may contain sensitive cookies and headers that could be used to impersonate you or your test account.

Configuration (use) | Playwright

This is the
recommended
approach for tests
without server-side state
. Authenticate once in the
setup project
, save the authentication state, and then reuse it to bootstrap each test already authenticated.

When to use

When you can imagine all your tests running at the same time with the same account, without affecting each other.

When not to use

Your tests modify server-side state. For example, one test checks the rendering of the settings page, while the other test is changing the setting, and you run tests in parallel. In this case, tests must use different accounts.
Your authentication is browser-specific.

Details

Create
`tests/auth.setup.ts`
that will prepare authenticated browser state for all other tests.

tests/auth.setup.ts
```
`import{testassetup,expect}from'@playwright/test';importpathfrom'path';constauthFile=path.join(__dirname,'../playwright/.auth/user.json');setup('authenticate',async({page})=>{// Perform authentication steps. Replace these actions with your own.awaitpage.goto('https://github.com/login');awaitpage.getByLabel('Username or email address').fill('username');awaitpage.getByLabel('Password').fill('password');awaitpage.getByRole('button',{name:'Sign in'}).click();// Wait until the page receives the cookies.//// Sometimes login flow sets cookies in the process of several redirects.// Wait for the final URL to ensure that the cookies are actually set.awaitpage.waitForURL('https://github.com/');// Alternatively, you can wait until the page reaches a state where all cookies are set.awaitexpect(page.getByRole('button',{name:'View profile and more'})).toBeVisible();// End of authentication steps.awaitpage.context().storageState({path:authFile});});`
```

`setup`
project in the config and declare it as a
dependency (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-projects#dependencies)
for all your testing projects. This project will always run and authenticate before all the tests. All testing projects should use the authenticated state as
`storageState`
.

`import{defineConfig,devices}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({projects:[// Setup project{name:'setup',testMatch:/.*\.setup\.ts/},{name:'chromium',use:{...devices['Desktop Chrome'],// Use prepared auth state.storageState:'playwright/.auth/user.json',},dependencies:['setup'],},{name:'firefox',use:{...devices['Desktop Firefox'],// Use prepared auth state.storageState:'playwright/.auth/user.json',},dependencies:['setup'],},],});`

user_input: How do I interact with a button that's rendered inside an iframe?
reference: Step into the frame with frameLocator and then locate as usual — the getBy* methods exist on FrameLocator, so you can chain: page.frameLocator('#my-frame').getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click().
llm_response:
To interact with a button inside an iframe, you must use a `FrameLocator` to target the iframe and then locate the button within it.

### Steps to interact with the button:
1. **Create a `FrameLocator`**: Use one of the following methods to target the iframe:
   - `page.frameLocator(selector)`
   - `locator.contentFrame()` (if you have a `Locator` pointing to the `iframe`)
   - `locator.frameLocator(selector)`

2. **Locate the button**: Once you have the `FrameLocator`, use `getByRole('button', ...)` to target the specific button.

3. **Perform the action**: Call `.click()` on the resulting locator.

### Example:
```javascript
// Using page.frameLocator()
await page.frameLocator('#my-frame').getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' }).click();
```

### Important Considerations:
* **Strictness**: Frame locators are strict. If your selector matches more than one frame, the operation will throw an error. If multiple frames exist, you must explicitly select the correct one (e.g., by using `.first()`):
  ```javascript
  await page.locator('.result-frame').contentFrame().first().getByRole('button').click();
  ```
* **Role Matching**: When using `getByRole`, you can specify the button's accessible name using the `name` option. By default, this is case-insensitive and searches for a substring. You can use the `exact` option to require a case-sensitive, whole-string match.

FrameLocator | Playwright

FrameLocator represents a view to the
`iframe`
on the page. It captures the logic sufficient to retrieve the
`iframe`
and locate elements in that iframe. FrameLocator can be created with either
locator.contentFrame() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-content-frame)

page.frameLocator() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-frame-locator)

locator.frameLocator() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-frame-locator)

```
`constlocator=page.locator('#my-frame').contentFrame().getByText('Submit');awaitlocator.click();`
```

Frame locators are strict. This means that all operations on frame locators will throw if more than one element matches a given selector.

```
`// Throws if there are several frames in DOM:awaitpage.locator('.result-frame').contentFrame().getByRole('button').click();// Works because we explicitly tell locator to pick the first frame:awaitpage.locator('.result-frame').contentFrame().first().getByRole('button').click();`

user_input: How do I split my tests to run across several machines at once?
reference: Shard with --shard=x/y — run 1/4, 2/4, 3/4 and 4/4 on four machines so each takes a quarter of the suite.
reference_contexts:
npx playwright test --shard=1/4
npx playwright test --shard=2/4
npx playwright test --shard=3/4
npx playwright test --shard=4/4
llm_response:
To split your tests to run across several machines, you use the `--shard=x/y` command-line argument. This divides your test suite into `y` parts, where `x` represents the specific shard index to be executed.

### General Usage
To run a suite in four shards, you would execute the following commands on different machines or jobs:
* `npx playwright test --shard=1/4`
* `npx playwright test --shard=2/4`
* `npx playwright test --shard=3/4`
* `npx playwright test --shard=4/4`

### CI Integration
You can automate this process within your CI pipeline configuration:

* **GitLab CI:** Use the `parallel` keyword to split jobs. You can use the built-in variables `$CI_NODE_INDEX` and `$CI_NODE_TOTAL`:
  ```yaml
  script:
    - npx playwright test --shard=$CI_NODE_INDEX/$CI_NODE_TOTAL
  ```
  Alternatively, use `parallel:matrix` to define specific shard values (e.g., `SHARD: ['1/10', '2/10', ...]`).

* **CircleCI:** Since CircleCI indexing starts at 0, you must add 1 to the index to match the `--shard` format:
  ```yaml
  - run: SHARD="$((${CIRCLE_NODE_INDEX}+1))"; npx playwright test --shard=${SHARD}/${CIRCLE_NODE_TOTAL}
  ```

* **Azure Pipelines:** Use a `strategy: matrix` to define the shards explicitly:
  ```yaml
  strategy:
    matrix:
      shard-1:
        shard: 1/3
      shard-2:
        shard: 2/3
      shard-3:
        shard: 3/3
  steps:
    - script: npx playwright test --shard=$(shard)
  ```

### Important Considerations
* **Parallelism:** Playwright can only shard tests that are capable of running in parallel. By default, this means Playwright shards test files.
* **Performance:** Sharding allows you to scale test execution across multiple machines simultaneously, which reduces total test runtime.
llm_references: Sharding | Playwright

```

Now, if you run these shards in parallel on different jobs, your test suite completes four times faster.

Note that Playwright can only shard tests that can be run in parallel. By default, this means Playwright will shard test files. Learn about other options in the
parallelism guide (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel)
.

```

`PROJECT`

```
Parallelism | Playwright

By default, Playwright runs test files in
parallel (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel)
and strives for optimal utilization of CPU cores on your machine. In order to achieve even greater parallelisation, you can further scale Playwright test execution by running tests on multiple machines simultaneously. We call this mode of operation "sharding". Sharding in Playwright means splitting your tests into smaller parts called "shards". Each shard is like a separate job that can run independently. The whole purpose is to divide your tests to speed up test runtime.

When you shard your tests, each shard can run on its own, utilizing the available CPU cores. This helps speed up the testing process by doing tasks simultaneously.

In a CI pipeline, each shard can run as a separate job, making use of the hardware resources available in your CI pipeline, like CPU cores, to run tests faster.

user_input: One test is genuinely slow and keeps timing out — is there a one-liner to give just it more room?
reference: Call test.slow() inside it; that marks the test slow and triples its timeout.
reference_contexts: test.slow() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-test#test-slow) marks the test as slow and triples the test timeout.
llm_response:
Yes, you can use one of the following one-liners inside your test:

*   **To triple the default timeout:** Use `test.slow();`.
*   **To set a specific duration:** Use `test.setTimeout(120_000);` (replacing `120_000` with your desired time in milliseconds).

reference: Test ids survive copy and role changes, so those tests keep passing even when the UI wording shifts — the downside is they aren't user-facing.
reference_contexts: Testing by test ids is the most resilient way of testing as even if your text or role of the attribute changes, the test will still pass. However testing by test ids is not user facing.
llm_response: Teams add `data-testid` attributes because it is the most resilient way of testing; the test will still pass even if the text or role of the attribute changes. Additionally, teams may use them when they choose to follow the test id methodology or when they cannot locate an element by role or text.
llm_references: Other locators | Playwright

Playwright comes with multiple built-in locators. To make tests resilient, we recommend prioritizing user-facing attributes and explicit contracts such as
page.getByRole() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-get-by-role)
.

For example, consider the following DOM structure.

http://localhost:3000
Sign in
```
`<button>Sign in</button>`
```

Locate the element by its role of
`button`
with name "Sign in".

```
`awaitpage.getByRole('button',{name:'Sign in'}).click();`
```

note
Use the
code generator (https://playwright.dev/docs/codegen)
to generate a locator, and then edit it as you'd like.

Every time a locator is used for an action, an up-to-date DOM element is located in the page. In the snippet below, the underlying DOM element will be located twice, once prior to every action. This means that if the DOM changes in between the calls due to re-render, the new element corresponding to the locator will be used.

```
`constlocator=page.getByRole('button',{name:'Sign in'});awaitlocator.hover();awaitlocator.click();`
```

Note that all methods that create a locator, such as
page.getByLabel() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-get-by-label)
, are also available on the
Locator (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator)
and
FrameLocator (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-framelocator)
classes, so you can chain them and iteratively narrow down your locator.

```
`constlocator=page.frameLocator('#my-frame').getByRole('button',{name:'Sign in'});awaitlocator.click();`
```

Testing by test ids is the most resilient way of testing as even if your text or role of the attribute changes, the test will still pass. QA's and developers should define explicit test ids and query them with
page.getByTestId() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-get-by-test-id)
. However testing by test ids is not user facing. If the role or text value is important to you then consider using user facing locators such as
role (https://playwright.dev/docs/locators#locate-by-role)
and
text locators (https://playwright.dev/docs/locators#locate-by-text)
.

For example, consider the following DOM structure.

http://localhost:3000
Itinéraire
```
`<buttondata-testid="directions">Itinéraire</button>`
```

You can locate the element by its test id:

```
`awaitpage.getByTestId('directions').click();`
```

When to use testid locators
You can also use test ids when you choose to use the test id methodology or when you can't locate by
role (https://playwright.dev/docs/locators#locate-by-role)
or
text (https://playwright.dev/docs/locators#locate-by-text)
.

warning
We recommend
locating by test id (https://playwright.dev/docs/locators#locate-by-test-id)
instead.

Playwright supports shorthand for selecting elements using certain attributes. Currently, only the following attributes are supported:

`id`
`data-testid`
`data-test-id`
`data-test`

```
`// Fill an input with the id "username"awaitpage.locator('id=username').fill('value');// Click an element with data-test-id "submit"awaitpage.locator('data-test-id=submit').click();`
```

note
Attribute selectors are not CSS selectors, so anything CSS-specific like
`:enabled`
is not supported. For more features, use a proper
css (https://playwright.dev/docs/other-locators#css-locator)
selector, e.g.
`css=[data-test="login"]:enabled`
.

If you absolutely must use CSS or XPath locators, you can use
page.locator() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-locator)
to create a locator that takes a selector describing how to find an element in the page. Playwright supports CSS and XPath selectors, and auto-detects them if you omit
`css=`
or
`xpath=`
prefix.

```
`awaitpage.locator('css=button').click();awaitpage.locator('xpath=//button').click();awaitpage.locator('button').click();awaitpage.locator('//button').click();`
```

XPath and CSS selectors can be tied to the DOM structure or implementation. These selectors can break when the DOM structure changes. Long CSS or XPath chains below are an example of a
bad practice
that leads to unstable tests:

```
`awaitpage.locator('#tsf > div:nth-child(2) > div.A8SBwf > div.RNNXgb > div > div.a4bIc > input').click();awaitpage.locator('//*[@id="tsf"]/div[2]/div[1]/div[1]/div/div[2]/input').click();`
```

When to use this
CSS and XPath are not recommended as the DOM can often change leading to non resilient tests. Instead, try to come up with a locator that is close to how the user perceives the page such as
role locators (https://playwright.dev/docs/locators#locate-by-role)
or
define an explicit testing contract (https://playwright.dev/docs/locators#locate-by-test-id)
using test ids.

The page.getByRole() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-get-by-role) locator reflects how users and assistive technology perceive the page, for example whether some element is a button or a checkbox. When locating by role, you should usually pass the accessible name as well, so that the locator pinpoints the exact element. For example, consider the following DOM structure. http://localhost:3000 Sign up Subscribe Submit ``` `

Sign up


` ``` You can locate each element by its implicit role: ``` `awaitexpect(page.getByRole('heading',{name:'Sign up'})).toBeVisible();awaitpage.getByRole('checkbox',{name:'Subscribe'}).check();awaitpage.getByRole('button',{name:/submit/i}).click();` ``` Role locators include buttons, checkboxes, headings, links, lists, tables, and many more (https://www.w3.org/TR/html-aria/#docconformance) and follow W3C specifications for ARIA role (https://www.w3.org/TR/wai-aria-1.2/#roles) , ARIA attributes (https://www.w3.org/TR/wai-aria-1.2/#aria-attributes) and accessible name (https://w3c.github.io/accname/#dfn-accessible-name) . Note that many html elements like `

Find an element by the text it contains. You can match by a substring, exact string, or a regular expression when using page.getByText() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-get-by-text) . For example, consider the following DOM structure. http://localhost:3000 Welcome, John ``` `Welcome, John` ``` You can locate the element by the text it contains: ``` `awaitexpect(page.getByText('Welcome, John')).toBeVisible();` ``` Set an exact match: ``` `awaitexpect(page.getByText('Welcome, John',{exact:true})).toBeVisible();` ``` Match with a regular expression: ``` `awaitexpect(page.getByText(/welcome,[A-Za-z]+$/i)).toBeVisible();` ``` note Matching by text always normalizes whitespace, even with exact match. For example, it turns multiple spaces into one, turns line breaks into spaces and ignores leading and trailing whitespace. When to use text locators We recommend using text locators to find non interactive elements like `div` , `span` , `p` , etc. For interactive elements like `button` , `a` , `input` , etc. use role locators (https://playwright.dev/docs/locators#locate-by-role) . You can also filter by text (https://playwright.dev/docs/locators#filter-by-text) which can be useful when trying to find a particular item in a list.

user_input: How do I watch the browser as my script runs and slow it down enough to follow along?
reference: Launch non-headless and pace each step with slowMo — e.g. chromium.launch({ headless: false, slowMo: 100 }).
reference_contexts:
// Chromium, Firefox, or WebKit
await chromium.launch({ headless: false, slowMo: 100 });
llm_response:
To watch the browser as your script runs and slow it down, you have two primary options:

**1. Recommended: UI Mode**
Playwright highly recommends using UI Mode for debugging, as it provides a better developer experience that allows you to walk through each step of the test and visually see what happened before, during, and after each step. It includes a watch mode and allows you to hover back and forward over each action.
*   **How to use:** Run the following command in your terminal:
    `npx playwright test --ui`

**2. Alternative: Headed mode with `slowMo`**
If you prefer to run the script directly, you can disable headless mode and add a delay to each operation.
*   **How to use:** Set `headless: false` and the `slowMo` option (in milliseconds) in your launch configuration:
    ```javascript
    await chromium.launch({headless: false, slowMo: 100});
    ```

user_input: My e2e tests mutate shared server state and run in parallel. What auth model avoids collisions, and how do workers stay on separate accounts?
reference: Give each parallel worker its own account and authenticate it once with a worker-scoped fixture. Key the account on the worker's parallelIndex — which stays the same even when a worker restarts — so a worker always maps to the same account.
reference_contexts: This is the recommended approach for tests that modify server-side state . In Playwright, worker processes run in parallel. In this approach, each parallel worker is authenticated once. All tests ran by worker are reusing the same authentication state. We will need multiple testing accounts, one per each parallel worker.

Each worker process is assigned two ids: a unique worker index that starts with 1, and a parallel index that is between 0 and workers - 1 . When a worker is restarted, for example after a failure, the new worker process has the same parallelIndex and a new workerIndex .
llm_references: Authentication | Playwright

This is the
recommended
approach for tests that
modify server-side state
. In Playwright, worker processes run in parallel. In this approach, each parallel worker is authenticated once. All tests ran by worker are reusing the same authentication state. We will need multiple testing accounts, one per each parallel worker.

When to use

Your tests modify shared server-side state. For example, one test checks the rendering of the settings page, while the other test is changing the setting.

When not to use

Your tests do not modify any shared server-side state. In this case, all tests can use a single shared account.

Details

We will authenticate once per
worker process (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel#worker-processes)
, each with a unique account.

Create
`playwright/fixtures.ts`
file that will
override storageState fixture (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-fixtures#overriding-fixtures)
to authenticate once per worker. Use
testInfo.parallelIndex (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testinfo#test-info-parallel-index)
to differentiate between workers.

user_input: Two problems with how our team writes tests. The recorder is the fastest way for people to get started, but the selectors it emits break on the next refactor, and half our app is behind a login so recording anything past the sign-in page means clicking through the form by hand every single time. Are both of these things the recorder can be told to handle?
reference: Both are, and they're separate mechanisms. On selectors: the generator isn't emitting raw CSS by accident — it inspects the page and picks what it judges the best locator, prioritising role, text and test id locators in that order, and when a candidate matches several elements it refines it until it uniquely identifies the target. So brittle output is usually a signal about the markup rather than the tool: give the elements you care about a test id (or accessible roles and names) and the recorder will prefer those. You can also use Pick Locator to grab and hand-tune a single locator rather than recording a whole flow. On the login: record the authentication once with `npx playwright codegen <url> --save-storage=auth.json`, which writes the cookies, localStorage and IndexedDB state at the end of the session, then start every later recording with `npx playwright codegen --load-storage=auth.json <url>`, which restores that state so the app comes up already signed in and you record only the part you care about. That saved state is the same kind of artifact your suite consumes as storageState, so the recorded flow and the running tests can share it.

This way, all cookies, localStorage and IndexedDB data will be restored, bringing most web apps to the authenticated state without the need to login again. This means you can continue generating tests from the logged in state.

The provided documentation addresses both of your concerns:

**1. Handling fragile selectors**
The test generator is designed to prioritize resilient locators, specifically role, text, and test id locators. If the generator identifies multiple elements matching a locator, it automatically improves the locator to uniquely and resiliently identify the target element. To further ensure stability, you can use `data-testid` attributes (or a custom attribute configured via `testIdAttribute` in your `playwright.config.ts`) to provide stable anchors for your tests.

**2. Handling the login form**
You can avoid manually clicking through the login form every time by preserving the authenticated state. There are two ways to handle this with the recorder:
*   **Save state:** Run `npx playwright codegen --save-storage=auth.json` to record the authentication step once and save the cookies, `localStorage`, and `IndexedDB` data to a file.
*   **Load state:** Once you have an `auth.json` file, you can use `npx playwright codegen --load-storage=auth.json <url>` to start the recorder already authenticated, allowing you to generate tests from the logged-in state without re-authenticating.

*   **Without `fullyParallel`:** Playwright defaults to file-level granularity. Shards are assigned entire test files, which can lead to imbalances if files are not evenly sized. In this case, you must manually organize test files to ensure balanced distribution.

`fullyParallel: true`
is enabled, Playwright Test runs individual tests in parallel across multiple shards, ensuring each shard receives an even distribution of tests. This allows for test-level granularity, meaning each shard will attempt to balance the number of individual tests it runs. This is the preferred mode for ensuring even load distribution when sharding, as Playwright can optimize shard execution based on the total number of tests.

Sharding without fullyParallel

Without the fullyParallel setting, Playwright Test defaults to file-level granularity, meaning entire test files are assigned to shards (note that the same file may be assigned to different shards across different projects). In this case, the number of tests per file can greatly influence shard distribution. If your test files are not evenly sized (i.e., some files contain many more tests than others), certain shards may end up running significantly more tests, while others may run fewer or even none.

Key Takeaways:

With
`fullyParallel: true`
: Tests are split at the individual test level, leading to more balanced shard execution.
Without
`fullyParallel`
: Tests are split at the file level, so to balance the shards, it's important to keep your test files small and evenly sized.
To ensure the most effective use of sharding, especially in CI environments, it is recommended to use
`fullyParallel: true`
when aiming for balanced distribution across shards. Otherwise, you may need to manually organize your test files to avoid imbalances.

GitHub Actions supports
sharding tests between multiple jobs (https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-jobs/using-a-matrix-for-your-jobs)
using the
jobs.<job_id>.strategy.matrix (https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/workflow-syntax-for-github-actions#jobsjob_idstrategymatrix)
option. The
`matrix`
option will run a separate job for every possible combination of the provided options.

The following example shows you how to configure a job to run your tests on four machines in parallel and then merge the reports into a single report. Don't forget to add
`reporter: process.env.CI ? 'blob' : 'html',`
to your
`playwright.config.ts`
file as in the example above.

First we add a
`matrix`
option to our job configuration with the
`shardTotal: [4]`
option containing the total number of shards we want to create and
`shardIndex: [1, 2, 3, 4]`
with an array of the shard numbers.
Then we run our Playwright tests with the
`--shard=${{ matrix.shardIndex }}/${{ matrix.shardTotal }}`
option. This will run our test command for each shard.
Finally we upload our blob report to the GitHub Actions Artifacts. This will make the blob report available to other jobs in the workflow.

.github/workflows/playwright.yml
```
`name:Playwright Testson:push:branches:[main,master]pull_request:branches:[main,master]jobs:playwright-tests:timeout-minutes:60runs-on:ubuntu-lateststrategy:fail-fast:falsematrix:shardIndex:[1,2,3,4]shardTotal:[4]steps:-uses:actions/checkout@v5-uses:actions/setup-node@v5with:node-version:lts/*-name:Install dependenciesrun:npm ci-name:Install Playwright browsersrun:npx playwright install--with-deps-name:Run Playwright testsrun:npx playwright test--shard=${{matrix.shardIndex}}/${{matrix.shardTotal}}-name:Upload blob report to GitHub Actions Artifactsif:${{!cancelled()}}uses:actions/upload-artifact@v4with:name:blob-report-${{matrix.shardIndex}}path:blob-reportretention-days:1`
```

After all shards have completed, you can run a separate job that will merge the reports and produce a combined
HTML report (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-reporters#html-reporter)
. To ensure the execution order, we make the
`merge-reports`
job
depend (https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-jobs/using-jobs-in-a-workflow#defining-prerequisite-jobs)
on our sharded
`playwright-tests`
job by adding
`needs: [playwright-tests]`
.

.github/workflows/playwright.yml
```
`jobs:...merge-reports:# Merge reports after playwright-tests, even if some shards have failedif:${{!cancelled()}}needs:[playwright-tests]runs-on:ubuntu-lateststeps:-uses:actions/checkout@v5-uses:actions/setup-node@v5with:node-version:lts/*-name:Install dependenciesrun:npm ci-name:Download blob reports from GitHub Actions Artifactsuses:actions/download-artifact@v5with:path:all-blob-reportspattern:blob-report-*merge-multiple:true-name:Merge into HTML Reportrun:npx playwright merge-reports--reporter html ./all-blob-reports-name:Upload HTML reportuses:actions/upload-artifact@v4with:name:html-report--attempt-${{github.run_attempt}}path:playwright-reportretention-days:14`
```

You can now see the reports have been merged and a combined HTML report is available in the GitHub Actions Artifacts tab.

user_input: Should I use a globalSetup file or project dependencies for one-time setup, and why?
reference: Prefer project dependencies. Because a dependency is a real project that runs ahead of the others, it plugs into the runner properly — the setup shows up in the HTML report, is traced, and can use fixtures — whereas globalSetup misses some of that.
reference_contexts: This is the recommended approach, as it integrates better with the Playwright test runner: your HTML report will include the global setup, traces will be recorded, and fixtures can be used.

Dependencies are a list of projects that need to run before the tests in another project run. They can be useful for configuring the global setup actions so that one project depends on this running first.
llm_response:
You should use **project dependencies**, as this is the recommended approach.

Project dependencies are preferred because they integrate better with the Playwright test runner, providing the following advantages over the `globalSetup` config option:

*   **HTML Report:** The setup is shown as a separate project in the HTML report.
*   **Trace Recording:** Full trace recording is available.
*   **Fixtures:** Playwright fixtures are fully supported.
*   **Browser Management:** You can use the `browser` fixture instead of manual management via `browserType.launch()`.
*   **Parallelism and Retries:** Supported via standard configuration.
*   **Config Options:** Options like `headless` or `testIdAttribute` are automatically applied.

In contrast, the `globalSetup` config option does not support trace recording or fixtures, is not shown in the HTML report, requires manual browser management, and ignores standard config options.

`globalSetup`
option in the
configuration file (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-configuration#advanced-configuration)
to set something up once before running all tests. The global setup file must export a single function that takes a config object. This function will be run once before all the tests.

Similarly, use
`globalTeardown`
to run something once after all the tests. Alternatively, let
`globalSetup`

`import{defineConfig}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({globalSetup:require.resolve('./global-setup'),globalTeardown:require.resolve('./global-teardown'),});`

user_input: Our app registers a service worker for offline support. Every route handler I install works fine against a build with the worker disabled, but against the real build some requests reach the network untouched while others are intercepted, and which is which seems to change between runs. What decides whether a request is interceptable here, and what's the sane way to test against this app?
reference: Whether a request is routable depends on who owns it. Once a service worker with a fetch handler is installed it sits between the page and the network: the page-owned request is served by the worker and never reaches the network, so it isn't routable, while the worker's own outbound request is a separate, service-worker-owned request that context routing does see. That split is why interception looks inconsistent — you're catching some requests at one layer and missing others at the other, and which layer serves a given resource depends on the worker's cache state, hence the run-to-run variation. If you're doing ordinary network mocking, the documented answer is not to reason about this at all: set `serviceWorkers: 'block'` in the config's `use` options so the worker never registers and everything is page-owned and routable. Only if you specifically need to assert on the worker's own traffic should you leave them enabled and branch inside the handler on `route.request().serviceWorker()` — noting that calling .frame() on such a request throws, and that requests for updated worker scripts cannot currently be routed at all.

Playwright provides built-in APIs for this use case that don't require the information below. However, if you're interested in requests made by Service Workers themselves, please read below.

user_input: Our GitHub Actions job installs cleanly — `npm ci` is green — and then every test fails at browser launch complaining about missing shared libraries. It's an ubuntu-latest runner, and the identical commit runs fine on all three of our developers' machines. What is the CI box missing that a laptop already has, and what's the durable way to fix it?
reference: Installing the npm package is not the same as provisioning a machine that can run browsers, and that's the gap. `npm ci` fetches the library; the browser binaries are downloaded separately, and those binaries need operating-system level libraries that a developer machine already has from everyday browser use and a bare Linux runner does not. So there are two things to install, and the combined step is `npx playwright install --with-deps`, which fetches the browsers and the OS dependencies together — that's exactly the step the recommended GitHub Actions workflow runs between `npm ci` and the test command. The alternative, and the more durable one if you also do visual comparison, is to run the job inside the official container image via `jobs.<job_id>.container`: it keeps the dependencies out of the host environment and gives you a consistent rendering environment, which matters because screenshots differ across platforms.
reference_contexts: Ensure CI agent can run browsers: Use our Docker image in Linux agents or install your dependencies using the CLI.
# Install NPM packages npm ci # Install Playwright browsers and dependencies npx playwright install --with-deps
The Command line tools can be used to install all operating system dependencies in CI.

GitHub Actions support running jobs in a container by using the jobs.<job_id>.container option. This is useful to not pollute the host environment with dependencies and to have a consistent environment for e.g. screenshots/visual regression testing across different operating systems.
llm_response:
The CI runner is missing the necessary system dependencies required to launch browsers, which are present on your local machines but not pre-installed on the `ubuntu-latest` environment.

To fix this durably, you have two supported options:

### 1. Install dependencies via CLI (Recommended for standard runners)
You must ensure the CI agent installs the required system dependencies alongside the browsers. Update your GitHub Actions workflow to use the following command:

```bash
npx playwright install --with-deps
```

This command installs both the Playwright browsers and the required OS-level shared libraries. Your workflow steps should look like this:

```yaml
- name: Install dependencies
  run: npm ci
- name: Install Playwright Browsers
  run: npx playwright install --with-deps
- name: Run Playwright tests
  run: npx playwright test
```

### 2. Use a Docker container
Alternatively, you can run your job inside a pre-configured Playwright Docker image. This ensures a consistent environment and avoids polluting the host runner with dependencies. You can configure this in your workflow file using the `container` option:

```yaml
jobs:
  playwright:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    container:
      image: mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.60.0-noble
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v6
        with:
          node-version: lts/*
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci
      - name: Run your tests
        run: npx playwright test
```

If you need to debug further, you can set the `DEBUG` environment variable to `pw:browser` to output logs during execution.

It's also possible to combine

user_input: Almost all of our tests stub the search endpoint so they're hermetic, and that's been great until the backend quietly renamed a field and every test stayed green while production broke. I want to keep most tests stubbed but have a couple that exercise the real endpoint and only override one flag in whatever comes back. Can the same interception mechanism do both, and what changes between them?
reference: Both go through the same route handler; what differs is whether you ever let the request reach the network. A hermetic stub never does: page.route(url, route => route.fulfill({ json: ... })) answers from the test and the server is never contacted, which is why a server-side shape change can't fail it. To modify a real response you have to fetch it first — inside the handler call `const response = await route.fetch()`, read the real body with `await response.json()`, mutate the field you care about, and then fulfill with the edited payload: `await route.fulfill({ response, json })`. That gives you the real contract for everything you didn't touch, so the renamed field would have surfaced. Routes are matched most-recently-registered first and are scoped to the page or context they were registered on, so a spec-level `page.route` override can sit on top of a project-wide stub. If you want the real traffic recorded once and replayed thereafter, that's what HAR replay is for.

Sometimes, it is essential to make an API request, but the response needs to be patched to allow for reproducible testing. In that case, instead of mocking the request, one can perform the request and fulfill it with the modified response.

In the example below we intercept the call to the fruit API and add a new fruit called 'Loquat', to the data. We then go to the url and assert that this data is there:

user_input: How does device emulation (viewport, user agent, touch) get applied per test, and why doesn't it bleed into other tests?
reference: Device parameters come from Playwright's device registry and are applied at the browser-context level. Since every test runs in its own isolated context — which can also carry mobile emulation, permissions, locale and color scheme — the emulation stays scoped to that test.
reference_contexts: Playwright comes with a registry of device parameters (https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/blob/main/packages/playwright-core/src/server/deviceDescriptorsSource.json) using playwright.devices (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-playwright#playwright-devices) for selected desktop, tablet and mobile devices. It can be used to simulate browser behavior for a specific device such as user agent, screen size, viewport and if it has touch enabled. All tests will run with the specified device parameters.

Browser contexts can also be used to emulate multi-page scenarios involving mobile devices, permissions, locale and color scheme. Check out our Emulation (https://playwright.dev/docs/emulation) guide for more details.
llm_response:
Device emulation (viewport, user agent, and touch) is applied by passing device parameters—such as those found in the `playwright.devices` registry—into the `use` configuration option. This can be done at three levels:

*   **Globally or per project:** By defining the `use` property within the `projects` array in `playwright.config.ts`.
*   **Per test file or describe block:** By using the `test.use({})` method.
*   **Manually:** When using the library directly, you can pass device parameters into `browser.newContext({...deviceParameters})`.

**Why it does not bleed into other tests:**
Playwright achieves test isolation by creating a new `BrowserContext` for every test. Because each test runs in its own isolated `BrowserContext` (which acts like an incognito-like profile), any emulation settings applied to one context do not affect others. When using the Playwright test runner, these contexts are created automatically for each test, ensuring that every test runs independently with its own specific configuration.

user_input: One fixture is slow, but I don't want to inflate every test's timeout. How do fixture and test timeouts relate, and what's the fix?
reference: A fixture's setup counts against the test's clock, so a sluggish one can trip test timeouts. Hand that fixture its own longer timeout through the tuple option and leave the test's timeout tight.
reference_contexts: By default, fixture (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-fixtures) shares timeout with the test. However, for slow fixtures, especially worker-scoped (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-fixtures#worker-scoped-fixtures) ones, it is convenient to have a separate timeout. This way you can keep the overall test timeout small, and give the slow fixture more time.

Fixture is considered to be a part of a test, and so its setup and teardown running time counts towards the test timeout. Therefore, a slow fixture may cause test timeouts. You can set a separate larger timeout for such a fixture, and keep the overall test timeout small.

```

worker-scoped (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-fixtures#worker-scoped-fixtures)
fixture has its own timeout, equal to the test timeout. You can change the timeout for a worker-scoped fixture in the same way.

user_input: Our CI machines are a lot slower than our laptops and I've been sprinkling per-assertion timeouts around to get the suite green, which is clearly the wrong shape. Some tests now fail with a message about the test itself rather than the assertion, and raising the assertion timeout further doesn't help those at all. How many separate budgets am I actually dealing with, and which one do I raise?
reference: Three budgets, nested, which is why raising the wrong one does nothing. The test timeout is 30 seconds by default and covers the whole test — the test function plus fixture setup plus beforeEach hooks — and it's what you're hitting when the failure names the test rather than an assertion; raise it in the config's `timeout`, or per test with test.setTimeout(120_000), or test.slow() to triple the default. Auto-retrying assertions like expect(locator).toHaveText() have their own separate 5-second expect timeout, which is unrelated to the test timeout and is the one reported in a 'expect.toHaveText with timeout 5000ms' call log; set it globally with `expect: { timeout: 10_000 }` or per assertion with a { timeout } option. Because the assertion budget is consumed inside the test budget, pushing the expect timeout above the test timeout accomplishes nothing — the test dies first. beforeAll/afterAll get their own timeout, equal to the test timeout by default and adjustable inside the hook. The right fix for a uniformly slower machine is the config-level defaults, not per-assertion overrides.
reference_contexts: Playwright Test enforces a timeout for each test, 30 seconds by default. Time spent by the test function, fixture setups, and beforeEach hooks is included in the test timeout.
Auto-retrying assertions like expect(locator).toHaveText() have a separate timeout, 5 seconds by default. Assertion timeout is unrelated to the test timeout.
export default defineConfig({ expect: { timeout: 10_000, }, });
test('very slow test', async ({ page }) => { test.setTimeout(120_000); }); test.slow(); // Easy way to triple the default timeout
beforeAll and afterAll hooks have a separate timeout, by default equal to test timeout. You can change it separately for each hook by calling testInfo.setTimeout() inside the hook.
llm_response:
You are dealing with multiple separate timeout budgets. Based on the documentation, the specific budgets are:

1.  **Test timeout:** 30,000 ms default. This covers the test function, fixture setups, and `beforeEach` hooks.
2.  **Expect timeout:** 5,000 ms default. This is for auto-retrying assertions and is unrelated to the test timeout.
3.  **Action timeout:** No default. Covers individual actions like `click`.
4.  **Navigation timeout:** No default. Covers navigation actions like `page.goto`.
5.  **Hook/Teardown timeout:** 30,000 ms default. Shared between fixture teardowns and `afterEach` hooks; also applies to `beforeAll` and `afterAll` hooks.
6.  **Fixture timeout:** No default (shares with test by default).
7.  **Global timeout:** No default. Covers the entire test run.

Since you are seeing errors about the test itself rather than the assertion (e.g., `Timeout of 30000ms exceeded`), you should raise the **Test timeout**. 

You can increase this in your config file:
```javascript
{ timeout: 60_000 }
```
Or override it for a specific test:
```javascript
test.setTimeout(120_000)
```

The assertion timeout is unrelated to the test timeout, which explains why raising it does not resolve errors caused by the test exceeding its own budget.

user_input: What's the reliable way to select a parent row based on a child element, and why avoid xpath=.. for it?
reference: Filter the parent by the child locator — e.g. getByRole('listitem').filter({ has: child }) — which is evaluated relative to the parent match. xpath=.. works but is brittle: any DOM change can break it, so prefer filtering.
reference_contexts: The filtering locator must be relative to the original locator and is queried starting with the original locator match, not the document root.

Alternatively, if you cannot find a suitable locator for the parent element, use xpath=.. . Note that this method is not as reliable, because any changes to the DOM structure will break your tests. Prefer locator.filter() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-filter) when possible.
llm_response:
The reliable way to select a parent row based on a child element is to use `locator.filter()`. You should use this method by passing the child locator to the `has` option of the parent locator.

**Example:**
```javascript
const child = page.getByText('Hello');
const parent = page.getByRole('listitem').filter({has: child});
```

You should avoid using `xpath=..` because it is not as reliable; any changes to the DOM structure will cause your tests to break. Additionally, XPath locators are tied to the implementation, whereas `locator.filter()` is preferred.
llm_references:
When you need to target a parent element of some other element, most of the time you should locator.filter() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-filter) by the child locator. For example, consider the following DOM structure: ``` `
    • ` ``` If you'd like to target the parent `
  • ` of a label with text `"Hello"` , using locator.filter() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-filter) works best: ``` `constchild=page.getByText('Hello');constparent=page.getByRole('listitem').filter({has:child});` ``` Alternatively, if you cannot find a suitable locator for the parent element, use `xpath=..` . Prefer locator.filter() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-filter) when possible. ``` `constparent=page.getByText('Hello').locator('xpath=..');` ```

Fixtures have a number of advantages over before/after hooks:

Fixtures
encapsulate

Fixtures are

`page`

Fixtures are
on-demand
- you can define as many fixtures as you'd like, and Playwright Test will setup only the ones needed by your test and nothing else.
Fixtures are
composable
- they can depend on each other to provide complex behaviors.
Fixtures are
flexible
. Tests can use any combination of fixtures to precisely tailor the environment to their needs, without affecting other tests.
Fixtures simplify
grouping
. You no longer need to wrap tests in
`describe`

user_input: Before a click, what does Playwright verify, and how does that relate to the waiting a plain click already does?
reference: A click runs actionability checks — attached, visible, stable, receives pointer events, enabled — and auto-waits for them. The pointer methods bake that same sequence in (down to scrolling into view), so you rarely need explicit waits.
reference_contexts: Playwright performs a range of actionability checks on the elements before making actions to ensure these actions behave as expected. It auto-waits for all the relevant checks to pass and only then performs the requested action. If the required checks do not pass within the given timeout , action fails with the TimeoutError .
wait for element with given selector to be in DOM
llm_response:
Before performing a `locator.click()`, Playwright verifies the following actionability checks:

*   **Resolution:** The locator must resolve to exactly one element.
*   **Visible:** The element must have a non-empty bounding box and not have a `visibility:hidden` computed style.
*   **Stable:** The element must maintain the same bounding box for at least two consecutive animation frames (i.e., it is not animating).
*   **Receives Events:** The element must be the hit target of the pointer event at the action point (i.e., it is not obscured by other elements).
*   **Enabled:** The element must not be disabled (e.g., it does not have a `[disabled]` attribute, is not part of a disabled `<fieldset>`, or is not a descendant of an element with `[aria-disabled=true]`).

Regarding the relationship to waiting, Playwright performs these checks automatically as part of its "auto-waiting" mechanism. It waits for all of these relevant checks to pass before executing the click. If these checks do not pass within the specified `timeout`, the action fails with a `TimeoutError`.

user_input: Where do downloaded files go, and why might they disappear before I can use them?
reference: Downloaded files sit in a temporary folder and belong to whichever context fetched them, so they vanish the instant that context is torn down. Each test gets a freshly created context, so grab anything you need before the test ends.
reference_contexts: Downloaded files are deleted when the browser context that produced them is closed.
Playwright uses browser contexts to achieve Test Isolation. Each test has its own Browser Context. Running the test creates a new browser context each time.
llm_response:
Downloaded files are initially stored in a temporary folder. You can specify a different location to persist these files by using the `downloadsPath` option in `browserType.launch()`.

Files may disappear before you can use them because all downloaded files belonging to a browser context are deleted when that context is closed. Additionally, if you handle the download event using `page.on('download')` without awaiting the operation, your script scenario might end while the download is still in progress, potentially leading to the context closing and the files being deleted.

Download (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-download)

page.on('download') (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-event-download)

All the downloaded files belonging to the browser context are deleted when the browser context is closed.

Note no await.constdownloadPromise=page.waitForEvent('download');awaitpage.getByText('Download file').click();constdownload=awaitdownloadPromise;// Wait for the download process to complete and save the downloaded file somewhere.awaitdownload.saveAs('/path/to/save/at/'+download.suggestedFilename());`
```

For every attachment downloaded by the page,
page.on('download') (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-event-download)
event is emitted. All these attachments are downloaded into a temporary folder. You can obtain the download url, file name and payload stream using the
Download (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-download)
object from the event.

You can specify where to persist downloaded files using the
downloadsPath (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsertype#browser-type-launch-option-downloads-path)
option in
browserType.launch() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsertype#browser-type-launch)
.

note
Downloaded files are deleted when the browser context that produced them is closed.

Here is the simplest way to handle the file download:

```
`// Start waiting for download before clicking. Note no await.constdownloadPromise=page.waitForEvent('download');awaitpage.getByText('Download file').click();constdownload=awaitdownloadPromise;// Wait for the download process to complete and save the downloaded file somewhere.awaitdownload.saveAs('/path/to/save/at/'+download.suggestedFilename());`
```

If you have no idea what initiates the download, you can still handle the event:

```
`page.on('download',download=>download.path().then(console.log));`
```

Note that handling the event forks the control flow and makes the script harder to follow. Your scenario might end while you are downloading a file since your main control flow is not awaiting for this operation to resolve.

reference: Video is flushed when the browser context closes. With the test runner that happens automatically, but if you created the context yourself you must await context.close(), or the file won't be written.

Video capture is tied to the browser context lifecycle because videos are saved upon the closure of the browser context at the end of a test.

user_input: We rolled our own visual checks: capture a PNG, compare it byte-for-byte with a committed file, fail on any difference. It's unusable — it fails on the first run of any new test, it fails constantly on CI with what look like anti-aliasing differences, and there's no way to accept a legitimate design change short of regenerating files by hand. What does the built-in comparison do differently at each of those three points?
reference: Each of your three problems is a thing the built-in assertion already handles, because capturing an image and asserting on one are different operations. page.screenshot() just returns a buffer; expect(page).toHaveScreenshot() is a full comparison assertion. On first run there is no baseline, so instead of failing meaninglessly it takes screenshots until two consecutive ones match — which also settles animation and rendering noise — saves the result as the reference and reports that it wrote it; you commit that file. On CI, the baseline is keyed by environment: the snapshot name like example-test-1-chromium-darwin.png encodes the browser and platform (the project name replaces the browser when you use multiple projects) precisely because rendering, fonts and anti-aliasing differ across platforms, so Linux CI compares against its own baseline rather than your macOS one. And byte-exactness isn't required: `maxDiffPixels` (per assertion or globally under `expect: { toHaveScreenshot: ... }`) sets an allowance. When a change is intentional you re-baseline with `npx playwright test --update-snapshots` rather than editing files.
reference_contexts: Error: A snapshot doesn't exist at example.spec.ts-snapshots/example-test-1-chromium-darwin.png, writing actual.

chromium-darwin - the browser name and the platform. Screenshots differ between browsers and platforms due to different rendering, fonts and more, so you will need different snapshots for them. If you use multiple projects in your configuration file, project name will be used instead of chromium.
Sometimes you need to update the reference screenshot, for example when the page has changed. Do this with the --update-snapshots flag. npx playwright test --update-snapshots
export default defineConfig({ expect: { toHaveScreenshot: { maxDiffPixels: 100 }, }, });
llm_response:
The built-in `toHaveScreenshot()` method addresses your three points as follows:

*   **First run of a new test:** Instead of failing, Playwright automatically generates the reference screenshot. It takes multiple screenshots until two consecutive ones match, saves the final result to the file system, and reports that it is writing the actual file.
*   **Anti-aliasing and minor differences:** Playwright uses the `pixelmatch` library for comparisons. You can configure the comparison tolerance by passing options such as `maxDiffPixels` to `toHaveScreenshot()`. This can be set per test or globally in your `playwright.config.ts` file to allow for minor rendering variations.
*   **Accepting design changes:** You do not need to manually regenerate files. You can update the reference screenshots by running the test command with the `--update-snapshots` flag (e.g., `npx playwright test --update-snapshots`).

user_input: In one test I need an admin and a regular user acting at the same time. How do I get two authenticated sessions side by side?
reference: Open two browser contexts in the same test, each seeded with a different storageState — one admin, one user — and drive their pages independently. Multiple contexts in one scenario is exactly how Playwright models multi-user features like chat, and they stay isolated.
reference_contexts: Use multiple BrowserContext (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsercontext) s and Page (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page) s with different storage states in the same test.
Playwright can create multiple browser contexts within a single scenario. This is useful when you want to test for multi-user functionality, like a chat.
llm_response:
To get two authenticated sessions side by side in a single test, you should use multiple `BrowserContext`s with different storage states.

### Recommended Approach: Using POM Fixtures
The documentation recommends using fixtures to provide pages authenticated as each role. This involves:

1.  **Defining Fixtures:** Create a file (e.g., `playwright/fixtures.ts`) that extends the base test to include `adminPage` and `userPage` fixtures. Each fixture creates a new `browser.newContext()` using a specific `storageState` file (e.g., `adminStorageState.json` and `userStorageState.json`) and initializes the corresponding Page Object Model.
2.  **Using Fixtures in Tests:** Import your custom `test` from the fixtures file and use the `adminPage` and `userPage` arguments in your test function.

### Alternative Approach: Manual Context Creation
If you prefer not to use fixtures, you can manually create the contexts within the test:

1.  Use `browser.newContext({ storageState: 'path/to/state.json' })` to create separate contexts for the admin and the user.
2.  Create a page for each context using `context.newPage()`.
3.  Interact with both pages independently.
4.  Ensure you call `await context.close()` for each context once the test is complete.

Both approaches rely on `browser.newContext()` to provide isolated, independent browser sessions.

user_input: We added an automated accessibility scan to the suite and it's been green for months. This sprint a screen-reader user reported that our settings panel now reads its sections in the wrong order after a refactor that only moved markup around — and the scan didn't say a word about it. What class of problem is that scan actually able to catch, what would have caught the regression, and can both live in the same test?
reference: The scan and the regression are aimed at different things, which is why one sailed past the other. An automated scan — the documented approach uses the @axe-core/playwright package, where you await `new AxeBuilder({ page }).analyze()` and assert the returned `violations` array is empty — detects *rule* violations such as missing or invalid properties. It has no opinion about whether the structure is the one you intended, and the docs are explicit that many accessibility problems can only be found through manual testing, recommending a combination of automated scans, manual assessment and inclusive user testing. What your refactor changed was the shape of the accessibility tree, and that is what an aria snapshot pins: expect(page).toMatchAriaSnapshot() captures a YAML representation of the accessibility tree — the hierarchy of accessible elements with their roles, attributes, values and text, with indentation carrying the nesting — and fails when the current tree stops matching it. Order and nesting are part of that representation, so a moved section shows as a diff. The two compose: accessibility tests are ordinary tests, so you can put both in one spec or keep separate ones. Bear in mind the tradeoff the docs draw between the styles — targeted assertions check one specific condition and get verbose over complex structures, while snapshots capture whole-structure state and are best for outputs that rarely change shape, which also means they need deliberate re-baselining when a change is intentional.
reference_contexts: The following examples rely on the @axe-core/playwright package which adds support for running the axe accessibility testing engine as part of your Playwright tests.

Automated accessibility tests can detect some common accessibility problems such as missing or invalid properties. But many accessibility problems can only be discovered through manual testing. We recommend using a combination of automated testing, manual accessibility assessments, and inclusive user testing.
Accessibility tests work just like any other Playwright test. You can either create separate test cases for them, or integrate accessibility scans and assertions into your existing test cases.

In Playwright, aria snapshots provide a YAML representation of the accessibility tree of a page. These snapshots can be stored and compared later to verify if the page structure remains consistent or meets defined expectations.

The YAML format describes the hierarchical structure of accessible elements on the page, detailing roles, attributes, values, and text content. The structure follows a tree-like syntax, where each node represents an accessible element, and indentation indicates nested elements.
Snapshot testing is ideal for: UI testing of whole pages and components. Broad structural checks for complex UI components. Regression testing for outputs that rarely change structure.
llm_response:
The automated accessibility scan (using `@axe-core/playwright`) is able to catch problems such as:
*   Poor color contrast between text and background.
*   UI controls and form elements missing labels.
*   Interactive elements with duplicate IDs.
*   Missing or invalid properties.

The regression you experienced—where the reading order of sections changed—would have been caught by **Snapshot testing** using `toMatchAriaSnapshot`. This allows you to assert the accessibility tree of a page against a predefined snapshot template, which would detect changes in the structure or order of elements as perceived by assistive technologies.

Yes, both can live in the same test suite. You can combine automated accessibility scans (using `AxeBuilder`) and accessibility tree snapshot assertions (using `toMatchAriaSnapshot`) within your Playwright tests to cover both automated rule violations and structural regressions.
llm_references: Snapshot testing | Playwright

Playwright can be used to test your application for many types of accessibility issues.

A few examples of problems this can catch include:

Text that would be hard to read for users with vision impairments due to poor color contrast with the background behind it
UI controls and form elements without labels that a screen reader could identify
Interactive elements with duplicate IDs which can confuse assistive technologies

The following examples rely on the
@axe-core/playwright (https://npmjs.org/@axe-core/playwright)
package which adds support for running the
axe accessibility testing engine (https://www.deque.com/axe/)
as part of your Playwright tests.

Disclaimer
Automated accessibility tests can detect some common accessibility problems such as missing or invalid properties. But many accessibility problems can only be discovered through manual testing. We recommend using a combination of automated testing, manual accessibility assessments, and inclusive user testing.
For manual assessments, we recommend
Accessibility Insights for Web (https://accessibilityinsights.io/docs/web/overview/?referrer=playwright-accessibility-testing-js)
, a free and open source dev tool that walks you through assessing a website for
WCAG 2.1 AA (https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/quickref/?currentsidebar=%23col_customize&levels=aaa)
coverage.

With Playwright's Snapshot testing you can assert the accessibility tree of a page against a predefined snapshot template.

```
`awaitpage.goto('https://playwright.dev/');awaitexpect(page).toMatchAriaSnapshot(`- banner:- heading /Playwright enables reliable end-to-end/ [level=1]- link "Get started":- /url: /docs/intro- link "Star microsoft/playwright on GitHub":- /url: https://github.com/microsoft/playwright- link /[\\d]+k\\+ stargazers on GitHub/`);`
```

By default, axe checks against a wide variety of accessibility rules. Some of these rules correspond to specific success criteria from the
Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/)
, and others are "best practice" rules that are not specifically required by any WCAG criterion.

You can constrain an accessibility scan to only run those rules which are "tagged" as corresponding to specific WCAG success criteria by using
AxeBuilder.withTags() (https://github.com/dequelabs/axe-core-npm/blob/develop/packages/playwright/README.md#axebuilderwithtagstags-stringarray)
. For example,
Accessibility Insights for Web's Automated Checks (https://accessibilityinsights.io/docs/web/getstarted/fastpass/?referrer=playwright-accessibility-testing-js)
only include axe rules that test for violations of WCAG A and AA success criteria; to match that behavior, you would use the tags
`wcag2a`
,
`wcag2aa`
,
`wcag21a`
, and
`wcag21aa`
.

Note that automated testing cannot detect all types of WCAG violations.

```
`test('should not have any automatically detectable WCAG A or AA violations',async({page})=>{awaitpage.goto('https://your-site.com/');constaccessibilityScanResults=awaitnewAxeBuilder({page}).withTags(['wcag2a','wcag2aa','wcag21a','wcag21aa']).analyze();expect(accessibilityScanResults.violations).toEqual([]);});`
```

You can find a complete listing of the rule tags axe-core supports in
the "Axe-core Tags" section of the axe API documentation (https://www.deque.com/axe/core-documentation/api-documentation/#axecore-tags)
.

user_input: I need to assert that every row in our pricing table renders right-aligned, which isn't in the DOM anywhere — it's a computed style. Nothing on the locator exposes it, and my first attempt at reaching into the page came back with undefined for the threshold I was comparing against, even though it's a plain number defined right above the call.
reference: Two boundaries are in play. First, to get at computed style you have to run code in the page: a locator resolves to elements but only exposes what the API models, so anything the API doesn't cover you obtain with evaluate. For the whole set at once use locator.evaluateAll(), whose callback receives the array of matching elements — e.g. `await page.locator('td.price').evaluateAll(els => els.map(e => getComputedStyle(e).textAlign))` — returning an ordinary array back into the test. Second, that callback executes in the browser, in a different context from your test file, so it cannot close over test variables; that's why your threshold was undefined rather than throwing at definition. Pass it explicitly as the second argument: `locator.evaluateAll((els, limit) => ..., limit)`. Whatever you return has to be serializable to cross back — return the strings or numbers you want to assert on, not DOM nodes.
reference_contexts: The code inside locator.evaluateAll() runs in the page, you can call any DOM apis there.
const rows = page.getByRole('listitem'); const texts = await rows.evaluateAll( list => list.map(element => element.textContent));

Evaluated scripts run in the browser environment, while your test runs in a testing environments. This means you cannot use variables from your test in the page and vice versa. Instead, you should pass them explicitly as an argument.
